A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same quantum entanglement-detection framework and retain corresponding state families, bandit policies, and proofs. All 20 pages of v1 and 29 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: Section V reports original simulations of measurement complexity and entanglement-detection rates, together with numerical counterexamples.

after.justification: Sections 6–7 report original simulator, real-device, and random-state results. Appendix A.4 adds an empirical readout-error-mitigation study.

M1.justification: The central witness criterion and Successive Elimination/lil’HDoC policies remain. Appendix A.4 adds a nested readout-mitigation procedure that periodically corrects measurement counts and uses those corrected counts in subsequent bandit updates. This is a limited procedural extension to the existing framework.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates isotropic/depolarized Bell states and arbitrary two-qubit states. V2 replaces the dedicated depolarized-state experiments with general Bell-diagonal-state evaluation on AerSimulator, noisy FakeBrisbane, and the physical ibm-brisbane device. These materially broaden the evaluated state population and measurement environments; arbitrary-state evaluation remains.

E2.justification: V1 has no quantitative tomography comparator. V2 Figure 4 introduces non-adaptive Bell-diagonal-state tomography at trace accuracies 0.01 and 0.05, using the copy-complexity bound derived in Appendix A.1. This adds a substantive comparison supporting the efficiency argument. Dai et al.’s witness-ordering methods are discussed but are not separately evaluated.

E3.justification: The arbitrary-state experiment increases from 500 to 1000 five-state instances, retaining the stated threshold of -0.001 and sample cutoff of 10^12. The new Bell-diagonal experiment uses a different five-state instance with three entangled states and measurement budgets of 10^6 per state on simulators and 10^5 on hardware. New protocols include tomography accuracy choices and mitigation intervals from 50 to 10000 shots.

E4.justification: V2 adds an analysis of how many witness bases are used under random ordering as the error tolerance varies (Figure 6). Appendix A.4 tests mitigation frequency against copy complexity and identification failures (Figure 7). These add substantial diagnostic and sensitivity evidence. The undetectable-state examples in v1 Table VI are retained as v2 Table 5.

E5.justification: V1 already reports 500-run averages and displays error bars. V2’s replacement Bell-diagonal experiments report 20 simulator runs and five hardware runs, explicitly discussing the hardware standard deviation and resource constraint. The mitigation study averages 20 runs. These revise repetition and uncertainty documentation without introducing confidence intervals or significance testing.

E6.justification: V1 Figures 2–3 are replaced by new backend and tomography comparisons in v2 Figure 4. The arbitrary-state detection curve also changes with the enlarged experiment. V2 adds witness-usage distributions, mitigation savings and failure regions, and the partial-transpose eigenvalue -0.029 for the retained mixed-state counterexample. These are new or replaced results under revised conditions, rather than demonstrated same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Appendix A.1 adds a tomography copy-complexity derivation and an accuracy condition preserving entanglement classification. Corollary 12 adds a bound for the two-witness workflow. V2 also generalizes the LIL lemma from unit subgaussian scale to sigma and specifies a paired-outcome estimator in Appendix A.2.1. Most original propositions and bandit proofs remain, with renumbering.

C1.justification: The main claims about the bandit correspondence, conclusive detection within F, and sample-complexity guarantees remain. V2 extends its contribution framing with explicit advantages over tomography and fixed-witness testing and an implemented experimental pipeline. The terms 'batch' and 'thresholding bandit' largely reframe the existing multi-state objective.

C2.justification: New discussion attributes copy savings to adaptive allocation and early stopping, explains how backend noise changes separability gaps, and argues why optimizing witness order separately for each state complicates batch detection. Appendix A.4 interprets mitigation failures as possible over-mitigation and identifies unresolved optimization questions. These substantially extend the interpretation beyond v1’s retained witness-family limitations.

D1.justification: V2 provides Bell-diagonal preparation and measurement circuits, probability-to-circuit parameter mappings, named simulation and hardware backends, shot budgets, Qiskit/MATLAB implementation information, and a code-repository reference. Appendix A.4 documents calibration, corrected-count updates, and mitigation scheduling. These substantially improve implementation and reproduction information absent from v1.

R1.justification: V2 substantially expands positioning against tomography, fixed-witness testing, and Dai et al.’s adaptive witness-ordering approach in Section 8. It adds relevant state-preparation, hardware, and readout-mitigation references, including Pozzobom and Maziero, Riedel Gårding et al., and Bravyi et al. This goes beyond citation-format changes to explain additional relationships with prior research.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and substantial preliminary and algorithm explanations are rewritten. State families become a separate section, implementation and arbitrary-state experiments receive distinct sections, and a new discussion precedes the conclusion. The appendix is reorganized around the baseline, proofs, and mitigation. This materially changes the narrative and document structure.

P2.justification: V2 adds circuit diagrams, the backend/tomography plot, witness-usage histograms, and a mitigation heatmap while replacing v1’s two dedicated sample-complexity plots. The phase diagram is redrawn, witness tables use abbreviated basis labels, and the witness-transformation table becomes inline content. Typography, headers, captions, and page layout are also extensively reformatted.

improvement.justification: V1’s practical case relied on abstract simulations without a quantitative tomography baseline. V2 addresses substantial implementation and validation gaps through circuits, code-access information, noisy and real-device experiments, and failure/sensitivity analyses. These materially strengthen reproducibility and practical evidence. The efficiency claims still need qualification: Figure 4 compares observed stopping counts with an accuracy-dependent tomography bound, hardware averages use only five runs, and Section 8.1’s polylogarithmic dependence on K overstates the bounds containing linear K factors.
